abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel intrinsic shape representation framework that fundamentally redefines how 3D models are characterized within the visual computing paradigm. Unlike conventional extrinsic approaches that rely on spatial embedding coordinates, our method leverages spectral graph theory to extract intrinsic geometric signatures that remain invariant under isometric deformations. We introduce the concept of manifold harmonic wavelets, which decompose shape geometry across multiple frequency bands while preserving intrinsic structure. The theoretical foundation establishes that these wavelet coefficients form a complete, orthonormal basis for the space of intrinsic shape features, enabling rigorous mathematical analysis of shape similarity and correspondence. Our analysis demonstrates that this paradigm shift resolves longstanding ambiguities in handling non-rigid deformations common in animation and shape analysis applications. The proposed framework provides provably correct correspondence establishment between arbitrary meshes without requiring landmark annotations. Experimental validation on standard benchmarks confirms the theoretical claims, showing that intrinsic methods outperform traditional approaches in both accuracy and robustness for shape matching tasks. This work opens new research directions for geometric modeling and computer vision by establishing intrinsic spectral analysis as a foundational theory rather than merely a computational tool.

We present a rigorous theoretical analysis of progressive photon mapping algorithms that yields significant improvements in convergence rates for photorealistic rendering. Our analysis identifies the fundamental limitation in existing unbiased estimators, revealing that photon density estimation suffers from systematic underestimation near specular surfaces. We derive novel mathematical bounds for the expected squared error as a function of photon count and kernel bandwidth, demonstrating that adaptive bandwidth selection based on local surface curvature can reduce estimation variance by an order of magnitude. The theoretical framework establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving consistent convergence in complex scenes with caustics and glossy interreflections. By reformulating the photon gathering process as a kernel density estimation problem on Riemannian manifolds, we obtain tighter bounds on bias introduced by non-Euclidean sampling. We prove that the proposed modified kernel function achieves asymptotically optimal mean integrated squared error under standard smoothness assumptions on the radiance field. This mathematical foundation enables principled parameter tuning that previously required extensive empirical testing. The improved theoretical understanding translates directly to practical rendering algorithms that achieve comparable visual quality with substantially reduced computational cost.

We introduce NeuralView, a groundbreaking system architecture for real-time 3D reconstruction and visualization that fundamentally rethinks the interaction between computer vision and computer graphics pipelines. Unlike traditional systems that treat reconstruction and rendering as separate stages, NeuralView employs a unified neural representation that simultaneously optimizes geometric accuracy and rendering quality. The system architecture comprises three novel components: a continuous neural implicit field for geometry representation, a differentiable rendering module for photorealistic output, and a sparse octree-based spatial indexing structure for efficient queries. This design paradigm enables unprecedented capabilities including dynamic topology changes, seamless level-of-detail transitions, and real-time relighting of reconstructed scenes. Our interactive technique leverages temporal coherence to maintain 60fps performance while processing live depth sensor input. The system demonstrates practical applications in augmented reality scenarios where physical and virtual content must be photorealistically integrated with consistent lighting and occlusion. We present an open-source implementation that supports standard RGB-D sensors and produces mesh outputs compatible with existing animation pipelines. This paradigm shift from sequential to unified processing represents a fundamental advance in how visual computing systems capture and represent real-world environments.

This paper presents an improved real-time fluid simulation and rendering system that achieves substantial performance gains over existing approaches through novel algorithmic optimizations and parallelization strategies. Our system addresses the computational bottleneck in pressure projection by introducing a hierarchical multigrid solver that adapts grid resolution based on local velocity divergence patterns. The rendering pipeline has been redesigned to exploit modern GPU architectures, achieving real-time performance for complex scenes with millions of animated particles while maintaining visual fidelity for animation applications. Key contributions include a memory-efficient particle encoding scheme that reduces storage requirements by 60% without sacrificing detail, and a temporal anti-aliasing technique specifically designed for dynamic fluid surfaces. The system implements an improved free-surface tracking algorithm using an adaptive height field representation that handles complex topological changes robustly. We demonstrate significant speedups on standard benchmarks, achieving interactive frame rates for scenes containing over 10 million particles. The visualization module provides real-time volume rendering with physically-based lighting models, enabling artists to iterate on simulation parameters with immediate visual feedback. Performance analysis confirms 3-5x speedup compared to state-of-the-art methods while producing visually indistinguishable results.
